author: Matt Rife
title: Autumn's First Major Nor'easter Takes Aim At The Mid-Atlantic And New England - NewsBreak
text:
By Matt Rife ,
21 hours ago AccuWeather A strengthening nor’easter is churning toward the upper Mid-Atlantic coast this weekend, bringing heavy rain, high winds, and severe coastal flooding after a quiet summer along the Atlantic seaboard.
States of Emergency are already active for New York City, Long Island, Westchester County, and coastal New Jersey. The system has already caused major beach erosion from North Carolina to New Jersey, and forecasters warn conditions will rapidly worsen from eastern Maryland to southern New England through Saturday night.
NOAA satellite imagery revealed an eye-like feature forming within the storm off the coast of North Carolina.
“This will be a long-duration event through multiple tide cycles well into this weekend, leading to major coastal flooding and beach erosion as well as strong winds pushing on trees for a longer period of time,” said Jon Porter, chief meteorologist at AccuWeather. “Expect not only coastal inundation from storm surge, but also areas of urban flooding away from the immediate coast, as well as regional power outages.”
The storm is expected to hook back toward the shoreline rather than drift out to sea. Strong high pressure sitting over the Canadian Maritime Provinces is forcing the system to turn toward New Jersey and southeastern New York instead of tracking toward southeastern Massachusetts, according to AccuWeather Senior Meteorologist Adam Douty.
Meteorologists warn the system could stall or make a slow loop between New Jersey and Long Island. While the track shares similarities with Superstorm Sandy in 2012, experts note that water level rises and storm surge are not expected to reach those historic extremes.
AccuWeather Still, coastal water levels from Virginia up to eastern Massachusetts could rise 2 to 3 feet above normal monthly high tides. Localized surges between 4 and 6 feet are possible in vulnerable bays and sounds. As winds shift to the north and northwest later in the weekend, trapped water inside bays could push against the back sides of barrier islands from Maryland to New Jersey, triggering extra flooding.
Rainfall totals will range from 1 to 4 inches from the Delmarva Peninsula into southern Maine. Coastal New Jersey, southeastern New York, and southern New England face the heaviest bands, with widespread totals of 4 to 8 inches and isolated maximums up to 13 inches. Because elevated tides slow down municipal storm drains, heavy downpours are expected to flood inland neighborhood streets blocks away from the ocean.
Wind gusts between 40 and 60 mph are forecast across the region, with peak gusts hitting 60 to 80 mph along exposed stretches of the coast. The combination of saturated soil and hours of relentless gusts poses a major threat to utilities.
“Persistent strong winds and saturated ground could bring down more trees than a faster-moving storm, increasing the risk of power outages,” Porter said. “Regional outages are possible in coastal areas from the Delmarva Peninsula through New Jersey to southeastern Massachusetts.”
The storm is also lingering over warm ocean water, which could alter its structure.
“The nor’easter will mimic a tropical storm in terms of impacts and still has the potential to actually evolve into a tropical storm as it will spend many hours over warm water,” AccuWeather Chief On-Air Meteorologist Bernie Rayno said.
Rough waters extend far beyond the storm’s center. Offshore seas are running between 15 and 30 feet, creating hazardous inlets for marine traffic along the Mid-Atlantic and New England. Farther south, large swells will fuel dangerous rip currents along beaches in North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida, even while inland areas from the Great Lakes to the Southeast see calm, sunny skies.
